item.title: Houthis push for control of Yemen highlands as Trump reportedly calls off airstrikes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Mohammed Ghobari and Jana Choukeir DUBAI, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Houthi fighters pushed to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Monday to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after a report that President Donald Trump had called off US strikes on the group at the last minute. A lightning advance by the Iran-backed ‌group this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies. Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown ‌Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen. The Houthis said on Saturday they had fired on Riyadh, where loud booms were followed by columns of smoke visible near the airport. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the first apparent strikes on ​the capital since the escalation began. The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared on Sunday to launch airstrikes against the Houthis after fresh pleas from the Saudi crown prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the airstrikes at the last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. The US military's Central Command referred questions to the White House. The White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. Trump spoke on Sunday to Rashid al-Alimi, president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, who asked him for US military help, four sources told Reuters. Two of the sources, one ‌Yemeni and one Western, said Trump made no direct pledge of military ⁠support during the call. FIGHTING IN HIGHLANDS The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen's capital since 2014, seized the country's Red Sea coast this month in an advance that routed forces of the Saudi-backed government. Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters' positions in the highlands, the Houthis say. According to the United ⁠Nations, nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the flare-up in fighting. Nearly 130,000 Yemenis have fled homes within Yemen, and more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa. Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kahboub Mountains, in two provinces, Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south. Fighting has centred on the outskirts of ​the ​remote mountain Al-Wazi'iyah district in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the mouth of the ​Red Sea that the fighters captured last week and the government's base in ‌Aden. The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab al-Mandab Strait leading into the Red Sea by taking control of the heights, according to the sources. That would let them open new fronts and help protect their new positions. SAUDI OIL EXPORTS The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis creates a dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington's Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched in February against Iran. The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since. The Houthis' newfound control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait risks cutting off the main alternative route that Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports that bypass disruption ‌in the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has responded by increasing shipments through Hormuz, where a small number of tankers ​are increasingly shuttling back and forth to bring out oil, charging record fees of as much as a quarter of the ​value of the cargo to brave the wartime risk. They then transfer the oil to ​other ships in the Indian Ocean, bound for customers in Asia or elsewhere. Satellite data shows Saudi exports through Hormuz reaching 2.9 million barrels per day in recent days, ‌up from just 700,000 in August, making up for a halt to Saudi ​loadings on the Red Sea. That has helped put a ​cap on the global price of crude oil, which has retreated closer to $100 a barrel after approaching $110 last week. But consumers and industry are still paying record prices for refined fuels. The US retail price of diesel, politically sensitive for Trump, hit another all-time high on Monday above $6.51 a gallon, from around $3.75 before the war began in February. In the latest reported attack in Hormuz, Britain's ​UKMTO maritime security agency said a ship sailing into the strait had ‌been hit with a projectile, causing minor injuries to crew. Diplomacy in the wider conflict has largely been stalled since a June interim agreement between the United States and Iran collapsed ​within weeks. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to fly on Tuesday to New York to attend the UN General Assembly, the first such visit since Trump launched "Operation Epic Fury" ​against his country alongside Israel in February. (Reporting by Reuters bureauxWriting by Peter Graff; Editing by Jon Boyle) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/houthis-push-control-yemen-highlands-110616361.html

item.title: He spent 11 months inside DOGE. Now he wants to set the record straight.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Tyler Hassen’s initiation into Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, started as a series of tests. The Houston oil executive says he was given vague instructions to show up at an unfamiliar D.C. address. He hastily packed three suitcases and flew east, taking an Uber to a building that he soon learned belonged to Elon Musk’s SpaceX. He was whisked to a private office, acutely aware that his tailored suit stood out among the hoodie-clad engineers “too locked in” to their laptops to look up. He was ordered to go through the website of the Department of Commerce and, within days, find two to five ideas to present to Musk. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. He checked into a nearby J.W. Marriott and told his wife he didn’t know how long he would be gone. Thus began an 11-month stint at the center of a national firestorm - an exhilarating, chaotic, and sometimes scary experience, Hassen told The Washington Post, in his first major interview detailing his forthcoming memoir and plans. The memoir, “Inside DOGE: The Real Story from a Senior Insider,” which recounts his time working for the secretive cost-cutting group, is the first tell-all to emerge from one of the most controversial periods of President Donald Trump’s time in office - a moment Hassen said he would gladly live through again. “There’s this misconception that we all just went in there and didn’t really think about what we were doing,” Hassen said, speaking virtually from a hotel room in San Diego. “I spent 24/7 thinking about it, waking up at three in the morning thinking, ‘Am I doing the right thing?’ … And I know I did.” At the heart of the book is a split screen: For many Americans, Musk’s project was a callous showcase of bending government to a billionaire’s will, associated with tens of thousands of federal layoffs, reams of lawsuits, an AI-enabled effort to kill off wasteful contracts, and the gutting of the U.S. Agency for International Development. But Hassen’s memoir enters a different vision into the historical record: He portrays a period marked by a clash in worldviews, in which hardcore capitalists are granted unprecedented power to change a system that they argue operates under completely different incentives, logic and norms. To Hassen, whose pre-government career involved turning around distressed companies, “DOGE was not radical,” he writes in the book. It was “not a wrecking ball, but a catalyst.” In conversation, Hassen comes across as mild-mannered, a distant temperament from Musk, who famously brandished a red metallic chainsaw as a metaphor for cutting government waste. A 43-year-old dad with Boy Scout energy, he doesn’t cut the image of the nerd-engineer DOGE bro. He spent his entire adult life “hiring, firing, reorganizing and rescuing failing businesses” in industrial manufacturing and the energy sectors - a skill set that appealed to Musk, his longtime deputy Steve Davis, and Baris Akis, a venture capitalist who served as a volunteer recruiter. But for years, he seethed with rage over the national debt, now at $40 trillion. He felt angry that the amount the U.S. spends annually just to service that debt is more than the government spends on national defense and many other public benefits. So he raised his hand - making a cold outreach to Musk through a network of business world connections, he said in the interview, and pressed the point. “I’m staring at my daughter, who is 5, and thinking about her at 25 with $100 trillion of debt. And I know if we don’t do something about it now, we’re going to be there ,” he said . “ We’ve got to fix it now. ” By its own accounting, DOGE fell far short of the $2 trillion Musk claimed he would save , and an independent report from the Government Accountability Office has found DOGE’s own savings figures to be flawed. But Hassen told The Post he believes the effort was a success. “Did we eliminate the deficit? No. Of course not,” he said. “But we made it on the top of everyone’s minds, albeit briefly, for a few months, that this deficit is something that we need to fix.” In the book, he argues that “DOGE fit squarely” within a tradition practiced by some Democratic presidents, from Bill Clinton to Barack Obama, who also sought to shrink bloated government. DOGE was different, he goes on to concede, because of its speed, “faster than Washington was ready for and faster than its defenses could absorb.” But Hassen insists that DOGE was not cruel, a word that appears six times in the memoir, often in relation to laying off federal workers. The refrain can read as a plea for reconsideration of an effort he argues was poorly understood. “In the private sector, there’s an understood bargain,” he writes. “You’re hired to create value. If the value disappears, so does the job. It isn’t personal. It isn’t cruel. It’s the operating system of capitalism.” Government, he argues in the book, runs on a different logic. Value is “presumed,” “permanence is the default,” and “the moral burden of proofs falls on anyone who questions headcount - no matter how bloated the system becomes.” After the screening process, Musk and Davis deployed Hassen to the U.S. Department of the Interior, a sprawling agency that manages roughly 500 million acres of federal land and property, national parks and tribal territories. He took the assignment, he wrote, because he knew “very little” about the agency and the challenge was appealing. Hassen was eventually promoted by Doug Burgum, the wealthy businessman who heads the agency, and who Hassen described as something of a kindred spirit. He became acting assistant secretary of policy, management and budget and stayed on until November - months after Musk himself had left Washington. During his tenure at DOGE, Hassen says he put in 14 hour days, working nights and weekends. During the chaotic period he only saw his then-four-year-old daughter a handful of times. He said he relished the minutiae of the job: pouring through grants written in what appeared to him to be bureaucratese, dissembling bloated org charts and consolidating departments. He says he encountered a bureaucracy more labyrinthine and redundant than he could have ever imagined. He caught spelling errors in a project description written by a vendor charging hundreds of millions of dollars, which he saw as proof of a systemic malaise. The contract, he writes, “stopped me cold.” (To drive home the point, a photo of the paperwork with the spelling error is published in the book). He told The Post he was exhilarated to get deep into the bowels of the bureaucracy and deploy his corporate-honed skill sets to attack a problem that had long troubled him. During his first week at DOGE, the team met in a sparse conference room on the top floor of the SpaceX offices - empty except for a giant American flag on the wall, “because it reminded us why we are here,” he told The Post. “We had billionaires to 22-year-olds who had dropped out of Harvard, all sitting there on our laptops working with public information - trying to figure out how we can help solve this deficit, this crisis that we’re in.” As the group grew, the meetings moved to the Eisenhower Executive Office Building. There, he told The Post that he would present to Musk on a weekly basis, receiving the world’s richest man’s undivided attention. “He has this ability to grasp so many things, from California water, to certain contracts,” he said. “We would talk about certain departments for 45 minutes - and how can we fix this - and we’d stay until two in the morning.” One time, after a particularly grueling session, Hassen said he had to sneak out of the White House grounds to sleep. “I was so tired,” he said. During his time at Interior, Hassen was almost like a Where’s Waldo character, popping up in key moments that caught the country’s attention. When wildfires struck California, Hassen made an unusual decision to fly to the state to grill local officials about why the state’s largest water plant wasn’t running at full capacity. The image of him at the Jones Pumping Plant in California became one of the first posts from the DOGE X account identifying its members - prompting a flood of hateful messages and threats to Hassen and his family, he said. When Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico, it fell to Hassen to officially register the rechristened Gulf of America in the Interior Department’s Geographic Names Information System - a move that then triggered a broader recognition of the name change on Google Maps and other online directories. Hassen says he felt the difference in mindset between the public and the private sector every day. “It showed up in the way career staff spoke about ‘the workforce’ as something apart - almost sacred,” he writes. “Until we can say out loud that government is a workforce like any other - noble in purpose, human in composition, and subject to reality like everything else - reform will look like cruelty before it looks like competence.” There is a clear cognitive dissonance between DOGE insiders like Hassen, who saw himself taking on a deeply patriotic project, and many Americans, who according to polls viewed DOGE disapprovingly. Not surprisingly, Hassen believes the media is one culprit - treating “every reduction as a moral offense” and framing DOGE leaders’ demands for accountability as a “cruelty experiment,” he writes. But, in the book Hassen reflects on how DOGE’s failure to communicate hurt its reputation. Though DOGE was announced with great fanfare - and its website broadcast tallied savings - in practice the project was highly secretive, with DOGE members often showing up in agencies wielding great power before ever appearing on an org chart. In the six months before the ill-fated cost-cutting effort imploded, its staff gave just a handful of interviews. Two, including one with Hassen, were on Fox News, and he told The Post he almost backed out. They were only done, Hassen writes, in response to prodding from then-White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt and Katie Miller, the political operative and podcaster who acted as a communications liaison for Musk’s effort. DOGE members were private citizens, fearful of being personally targeted and unfamiliar with the media apparatus that is part of Washington culture, he says. But, fundamentally, the DOGE crew wanted to stay completely focused on the mission itself, he writes. The team was well aware that they needed to move with speed, as they might soon be slowed down by lawsuits, Congress or other bureaucratic forces. “We were there to work. We weren’t there to be public figures,” he said in the interview. In the book, Hassen implies that this was, to some degree, a miscalculation. “Once we stepped back, others were happy to define the work for us.” Ultimately, DOGE did lose control of the narrative, leading to a dramatic split between Trump and Musk five months after DOGE began and leaving the project in the lurch. The night of that split, Hassen said he paced around the Interior Department like a ghost. The next morning, he went to the agency gift shop and bought his daughter a T-shirt which said “Future Secretary of the Interior.” He thought it might be his last night in D.C. Hassen’s experience working with AI for the first time at DOGE led him to take a new job leading Zone Frontier, a former cleaning supply firm with a new mission to provide infrastructure and permitting to the data center industry. Musk’s longtime lawyer, Alex Spiro, has also joined the board of directors, something Hassen said was a pure coincidence . He says he hopes that the legacy of DOGE will be that the country’s most gifted citizens will seek to serve their government. Instead of draining the swamp, he says he wants to flood it with talent and energy. “These are some of the best and brightest we have in America,” he said of the DOGE team. “I’m honored to be even a part of them.” Faiz Siddiqui contributed to this report. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/09/21/he-spent-11-months-inside-doge-now-he-wants-set-record-straight/

item.title: Nvidia CEO rejects AI 'doomsday' scenarios and pushes back on new rules
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang told CBS News he disagrees with recent warnings from artificial intelligence researchers that the technology could lead to humanity's extinction within a few years, calling such statements overblown "doomsday narratives." "2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world," Huang told CBS News senior business and technology correspondent Jo Ling Kent ON Friday. "Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible." Huang was responding to claims on social media by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon earlier this month that AI developers "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." Coxon's remarks sparked heated public debate about the risks posed by AI, as well as calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and other leading industry figures to slow development of the technology. But Huang said he rejects such predictions because they are "not grounded in science." Nvidia has a substantial stake in the debate, given that its specialized chips power the large language models (or LLMs) by which artificial intelligence agents, created by OpenAI and others, access and synthesize information. Demand for those chips has boosted Nvidia's market value to $5.3 trillion, making it the world's most valuable company. Asked why Americans should trust him on AI safety, given his company's incentives, Huang told CBS News that it's in Nvidia's best interest to ensure the industry builds its products responsibly. "Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services," he said. "If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished." No need for AI rules? Several recent security breaches have spurred calls for AI regulation, including a July incident in which OpenAI bots went rogue and hacked the AI company Hugging Face . On Thursday, OpenAI also disclosed six additional incidents it described as "unexpected or concerning" behavior involving its AI models, prompting some lawmakers to call for tighter oversight of AI developers. Huang dismissed the need for new regulations, saying that existing U.S. laws governing product liability and unauthorized entry are sufficient. He added that he agrees with President Trump's view that the AI industry doesn't need additional guardrails. "You have all kinds of liabilities associated with cybersecurity" and damage liability laws, Huang said. "Apply that first — don't let this doomsday narrative allow someone to relieve them of the laws that currently exist." Competing with China In pushing back against calls for a freeze in developing frontier AI models, Mr. Trump has warned that such a slowdown could give China an edge as the world's two biggest economies compete in a critical new tech sector. Nvidia has been caught in the crosshairs of that battle, with the federal government restricting it from selling certain types of chips to China. Last December, Mr. Trump allowed Nvidia to start selling its H200 computer chips to "approved customers" in China. But the U.S. still bars the company from selling its most advanced chips (including those used to power AI models) in China. Huang said he believes technology created in America should benefit the U.S. first. But he takes issue with government bans on the sale of U.S. tech in China. "Every single chip company should go and serve the world, compete for the world," he said. "That's all about competing. America is about competition." Huang, who will attend a White House dinner on Sept. 24 where Mr. Trump will host Chinese President Xi Jinping, said he wants to speak with Xi about setting global standards for AI development. Chinese leaders "want China to have the benefit of AI. They want China to prosper, just as we want America to prosper," Huang said. "Don't you wish every country would have aspirations for a better tomorrow? And I love that about them." Huang noted that there are some areas where American AI companies would not be able to work with China, such as national security or defense. Why Huang defends data centers Asked about the widespread public concerns about data centers in the U.S., Huang said he believes the AI industry made some missteps as the buildout was taking off. "I would say we're sorry we didn't come talk to you sooner," Huang said of addressing communities where voters are pushing back against data centers. "We need to go engage the communities long before we set up the data centers." Data centers have evolved from their early days, becoming more energy-efficient and requiring less water to operate, while also boosting job growth and local economic activity, according to Huang. Building data centers can help "bring back building and manufacturing again," he said. Where Huang stands on taxes Huang's net worth stands at $182 billion, ranking him as the eighth-wealthiest person in the world, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Voters in his home state of California will vote on a billionaires' tax this fall, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on Californians with net worths of $1 billion or more. While other California billionaires have criticized the proposal, Huang said he doesn't object to paying billions of dollars in additional taxes if the measure passes in November. "The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege," Huang said. "I feel it's a privilege. It's a responsibility. And nothing would give me more joy than to be able to pay even more taxes." He added, "I'm not afraid of paying taxes — I'm just afraid of being poor." Huang also referred to himself as "the ultimate American dream" and credited the U.S. with fostering the educational and professional opportunities that enabled him to become an entrepreneur. Huang said he was working as a dishwasher at Denny's when he came up with the idea for Nvidia, and never dreamed that he would one day be at the forefront of the AI industry. "I was just really, really focused on doing dishes like no dishwasher ever did dishes," he said. WEB EXCLUSIVE: Watch an extended interview with Jensen Huang (Video) Story produced by Emily Pandise and Sari Aviv. Editor: Emanuele Secci. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jensen-huang-nvidia-rejects-ai-extinction-warnings/

item.title: Tesla faces major trial for alleged bias against Black workers after years of lawsuits
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Daniel Wiessner Sept 21 (Reuters) - A California agency's lawsuit accusing Tesla of allowing rampant race discrimination at its flagship assembly plant is set to go to trial on Monday, one of a ‌series of similar lawsuits being faced by the electric vehicle maker. Lawyers for Tesla and the California ‌Civil Rights Department will square off in Oakland before state Superior Court Judge Peter Borkon, who has scheduled the trial to run until October ​30. In the lawsuit filed in 2022, the California Civil Rights Department claims Black workers at Tesla's Fremont, California plant were subjected to pervasive harassment by other employees, including racial slurs and graffiti, and Tesla failed to prevent or stop it. Tesla is also accused of paying Black workers less than others and depriving them of opportunities for promotions. Tesla and ‌its lawyers did not respond to requests ⁠for comment. The company has denied wrongdoing and said that it does not tolerate discrimination and has fired workers found to have engaged in misconduct. The California Civil Rights Department's director, ⁠Kevin Kish, in a statement said the agency looked forward to holding Tesla accountable. Tesla's high profile and the thousands of workers involved in the case make it among the most significant involving employment discrimination claims against a major US company to ​go ​to trial in recent years. NO CAP ON DAMAGES Borkon has scheduled ​a bench trial, meaning that he and not ‌a jury will decide whether Tesla is liable for violations of California civil rights laws. Unlike federal law, the California law barring workplace discrimination does not cap the damages a court can award to affected workers, and Tesla could be on the hook for many millions of dollars if it loses the case. Tesla has for the last decade been dogged by claims that it fostered a climate at the Fremont plant and other facilities that was extremely ‌hostile to Black workers. The company is also facing a lawsuit ​from the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission alleging racial harassment, and ​dozens of lawsuits by individual workers making similar ​claims. The claims in the Civil Rights Department's lawsuit are broader and include allegations that the ‌Fremont plant was racially segregated, with Black workers ​assigned to the lowest-paying and ​least desirable jobs. Borkon ruled in a separate lawsuit last year that more than 6,000 Black workers could not sue Tesla as a class, reversing an earlier decision and handing a major victory to the company. Tesla ​has settled some of the individual ‌lawsuits, including one by a former elevator operator at the Fremont plant who was awarded $137 million by ​a jury, a sum that was later slashed by a judge. (Reporting by Daniel Wiessner in ​Albany, New York, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Rosalba O'Brien) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/tesla-faces-major-trial-alleged-100649614.html

item.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue Trump over White House press ban
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Three news organizations whose journalists were banned from the White House last week are suing President Donald Trump and three top advisers, calling the abrupt lockout a “direct assault on the First Amendment.” POLITICO, CNN and MS NOW said in a joint statement Monday that they are bringing the federal lawsuit in a bid to immediately restore access for their reporters, who were denied entry to the White House complex on Saturday and had their credentials confiscated by the Secret Service. “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the news organizations said. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” The organizations filed the suit Monday in U.S. District Court in Washington. They are asking a judge to quickly rule Trump’s ban unconstitutional and prevent his aides from enforcing it. Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post attacking the news media outlets. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social early Monday. “It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” The White House’s exclusion of the journalists followed an announcement from Trump on Friday that he was banning reporters for the three outlets “effective immediately.” Trump’s post Friday was vague about the reasons for the ban , beyond complaining about “constant ‘reporting’” of what he called “FICTION and LIES.” Questioned about the move during an Oval Office photo op, Trump offered few specifics. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it,” Trump said. “They’re smart people, but they purposely write negative news.” The news organizations, represented by Theodore Boutrous Jr. of law firm Gibson Dunn, are filing suit against Trump, chief of staff Susie Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and Secret Service Director Sean Curran. The news outlets argue that the president’s ban violates the Constitution in multiple ways: The abrupt cancellation of White House access without notice violated the organizations’ Fifth Amendment due process and property rights, and the retaliation for the content of their reporting violated their First Amendment rights. The suit contends that the ban is already “severely impeding” the news organizations’ ability to report on the Trump White House while also causing a chilling effect among other news outlets, who could find themselves similarly locked out if the president deems their coverage “insufficiently favorable.” “The President’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO from the White House is a direct assault on the First Amendment and a blatant violation of due process,” Boutrous said in a statement. “The President has been explicit that this ban is intended to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to intimidate journalists and news organizations covering him and his administration. This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the President of the United States. The law is on our side across the board, and we look forward to presenting our arguments to the court as soon as possible.” Though long-standing legal precedents permit the White House to restrict journalists’ access to the building, courts have ruled that officials can’t apply those restrictions in ways that discriminate based on viewpoint or content. Previous efforts by Trump to deny access to specific reporters or news organizations have run into resistance in the courts, although the most recent litigation led to a muddled result. In 2018, during Trump’s first term, officials suspended the White House hard pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta, with officials contending he kept speaking and clung to the microphone after Trump made clear he was moving on to another reporter. A judge ordered Acosta’s credential restored , citing a murky process surrounding the suspension. A similar fight played out the following year, after a verbal altercation in the Rose Garden between a freelance journalist for Playboy, Brian Karem, and Trump adviser Sebastian Gorka. A federal judge ordered the White House to return Karem’s credential , concluding that the rules of decorum for such events were not clear enough to provide due process. Last year, another legal clash erupted after Trump barred the Associated Press from attending East Room events and kicked the wire service out of the White House press pool, the small group of reporters routinely given access to the Oval Office, Air Force One and other sensitive locations frequented by the president. Trump’s action came after the AP refused to adopt Gulf of America, after he signed an executive order renaming the body of water long known as the Gulf of Mexico. Though a federal district judge sided with the AP , the bulk of his ruling was temporarily put on hold by a panel of the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found the most restricted areas such as the Oval Office and Air Force One were not subject to the broader First Amendment protections of the rest of the complex. “These restricted presidential spaces are not First Amendment fora opened for private speech and discussion,” the panel’s majority wrote . “The White House therefore retains discretion to determine, including on the basis of viewpoint, which journalists will be admitted.” Although the appeals court’s June 2025 ruling was a preliminary one, it allowed Trump to follow through with his attempt to ban the AP from the Oval Office. The AP asked the D.C. Circuit’s full bench to take up the issue, but a majority of the court’s judges declined to do so . Arguments aimed at a definitive ruling on the AP’s lawsuit took place before a three-judge panel last November . The court has yet to rule. The D.C. Circuit ruled almost a half-century ago in a case involving Nation magazine reporter Robert Sherrill that journalists can’t be denied access to the White House arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting. Megan Messerly contributed to this report. CORRECTION: An earlier version of this report misspelled Theodore Boutrous Jr.'s name.This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/news-outlets-trump-banned-white-100906525.html

item.title: Russia lured Ukrainian teens to launch attacks. Now they're in prison.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
KREMENCHUK, Ukraine - Yaroslav Suzanskyi was 16 when he saw an ad on the Telegram messaging app offering “easy money,” about $165, to do an odd job. It turned out to be a want-ad for sabotage: Suzanskyi was paid to set fire to a railway relay cabinet. Now 18, Suzanskyi is incarcerated at a juvenile correctional colony, both a perpetrator and a victim of a hidden part of Russia’s war against Ukraine: recruiting vulnerable young people to attack their own country. He is one of eight inmates at Kremenchuk - in a population of 72 - convicted of national security or public safety offenses linked to Russia. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Many of the children recruited by Russia are impoverished and are lured into betraying Ukraine with relatively small offers of money, the authorities said. After torching the railway equipment, Suzanskyi got a bigger offer involving an explosive, for 60,000 hryvnias, or about $1,430. A man Suzanskyi knew as Artem sent him to a hotel in the Kyiv suburbs, where two backpacks were left outside Suzanskyi’s room. One contained military clothing, the other a taped box with wires that Suzanskyi thought was a jammer but later learned was an explosive device. He was then sent by taxi to a library. Ukrainian intelligence officers intercepted him there before he could complete the assignment. “Those 60,000 turned into five years,” Suzanskyi said. Suzanskyi was 13 when Russia’s full-scale invasion began. His father and stepfather were drafted, leaving his mother to support three children. A bureaucratic mistake stopped the family’s child-support payments, and they fell behind on bills, he said. He began taking whatever work he could find. In December 2024, with his younger brother’s birthday and the winter holidays approaching, Suzanskyi said he had just 200 hryvnias, or about $5, left. That’s when he responded to the ad on Telegram. Across Ukraine, 13 minors are serving sentences in Russia-related cases, including five girls, according to the Justice Ministry. In all, more than 300 juveniles have been detained on similar charges, officials said. Some received probation, while others are still under investigation. A report published last year by the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights noted “a surge in credible allegations that the Russian Federation used Ukrainian children in Government-controlled territory to conduct surveillance and transmit information on the Ukrainian military, or to commit sabotage and arson targeting military objects or public property with links to the military.” Russia denies the allegations and has blamed Ukrainian intelligence services for recruiting Russian minors to carry out sabotage in Russia. Oleksii Babakov, now 17, spent about eight months under Russian occupation in Vovchansk, on the Russian border, where he was living in foster care. When he was 15, guardians helped get him to Kharkiv and eventually to live in Poland, which is when he saw a Telegram ad promising easy money. Babakov was asked to recruit other young people and pass them on to a handler. One was Vikentii, now also 17, a friend of Babakov’s from when they attended a cadet corps together in Kharkiv in 2022. Vikentii spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his first name because of fear that he will be targeted for retaliation. Babakov told him that he could earn up to $3,000 a month. At first, Vikentii said, he thought he would only have to make explosive devices. Later, he learned that he was also expected to plant one. He was 15 at the time. He left the device in a trash bin outside a police station in Kharkiv and walked away. “When I blew up the bomb, I understood that I had done a really bad thing,” he said. He later saw a report that no one had been hurt. “I felt relieved,” he said. “There’d been a terrorist attack, but no one was hurt.” From Poland, Babakov saw news reports about people he had recruited. One was Vikentii. Another was a 15-year-old girl who left an explosive device outside a different police station. No one was hurt in that blast either. Ukrainian authorities tracked down Babakov in Poland, and he was deported to Ukraine. He and Vikentii met again in a pretrial detention center and are now serving their sentences together in Kremenchuk. Vikentii was convicted of committing a terrorist act and sentenced to three years in prison. Babakov was convicted of inciting and assisting a terrorist attack and sentenced to four years. Maksym Parshyn, 17, is from Slovyansk, in the eastern region of Donetsk that Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to surrender. Parshyn’s mother has schizophrenia, and his family has struggled financially. Parshyn said legitimate employers were reluctant to hire him because he was too young. For a while, he loaded firewood and worked for illegal call centers scamming people in Russia. “It’s very easy,” Parshyn said of finding work on Telegram. “You write something like ‘find work,’ and it’s all there.” Parshyn accepted $300 from an anonymous Telegram contact he described as a “handler” to set fire to a railway relay cabinet. The next day, the same contact offered him more money to burn vehicles used by military recruitment officers. Parshyn said he refused and blocked the account. A few weeks later, however, he accepted another offer to spray-paint graffiti on a military recruitment office. Months later, he returned to Telegram where a new handler had offered him $3,000 to set fire to a post office. Parshyn filmed while one of his friends set the fire. Parshyn said he did not realize until he was detained that Russian intelligence services were using Telegram to recruit young Ukrainians for such attacks. He spent about a year in pretrial detention before being sentenced to four years. “I needed money,” Parshyn said. “If I hadn’t needed it, I wouldn’t have done it at all.” After turning 18, teenagers can remain in Kremenchuk for education and rehabilitation until age 22 or they may be transferred to adult facilities. Deputy Justice Minister Yevhen Pikalov said the boys detained in Kremenchuk were motivated by money not treason. “They did not do it with the motive of destroying the Ukrainian state,” Pikalov said. “They didn’t do it because they love Russia. $500 on Telegram, that’s it.” In the colony, personal phones are not allowed. Staff hold the boys’ SIM cards, and calls and video calls go through the institution. Computers and tablets are supervised, and social media is blocked. During free time, the boys play sports, read, watch television or use a PlayStation. Money from family or earned inside the facility can be spent at the colony shop. In Kremenchuk, as everywhere in Ukraine, life is overshadowed by Russian airstrikes. Blast waves from nearby missile attacks have damaged the colony three times, but the detainees were in shelters, and no one was hurt, staff said. Air-raid alerts frequently interrupt classes at the school. When The Washington Post visited on July 20, one room, normally used for table tennis, was set up for Ukraine’s university entrance exam the next day. In another, chess and checkers boards came out. A few sat down to play while others chatted. A key question for all of the boys is: What comes next? Pikalov said that judging whether a youth has been rehabilitated depends on each teenager’s risks and needs rather than the offense they committed. Babakov dreams of a “clean slate.” Parshyn said he wants to hug his family after getting out. For Suzanskyi, that next step has already begun. He has started an online university degree in agronomy. After turning 18 in June, Suzanskyi chose to transfer to a more restrictive medium-security prison for adult men, rather than remain in Kremenchuk. “To try adult life,” he said, “so I definitely won’t want to end up in prison again.” On Aug. 11, he left Kremenchuk. With 3½ years still to serve, what worries him most is what might happen to his family as Russian attacks intensify. “I’m afraid there simply won’t be any relatives left by the time I get out,” he said. item.title: Gas prices are higher than they've ever been at this point in recent election cycles
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Another leg up in gas prices to begin September underscores the political headwind that President Trump and Republicans face on the issue, with less than seven weeks left before the midterm elections. The average price of US regular gasoline was $4.32 per gallon last Monday, according to the latest weekly data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) , a nearly $0.25 rise over the last two weeks. The EIA data, which goes back to 1990, also shows that gas prices are the highest they've ever been at this stage in any recent election cycle, according to a Yahoo Finance analysis. The second-highest price on record at this point — 49 days from an election — came in 2012 when gas cost $3.88 per gallon. The third-highest price was $3.65 in 2022. Both were election years when a Democratic administration was in power, and Republicans put a heavy focus on the issue of pump prices. "Gas prices are at crazy levels--fire Obama!" then private citizen Donald Trump posted to social media back in 2012 . With Trump now in office, gas prices are being pushed up by a variety of factors, including both the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and they're hitting as Trump has few options to lower them due to widening disruptions in the Middle East and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at historically low levels after months of withdrawals. Diesel, which broke through all-time high prices earlier this month and hit another record high last Tuesday , is yet another economic headwind. 'Anything but a typical year' The historical data also shows that prices tend to decline in the run-up to election day — in keeping with fall trends — but this year may be an outlier. Nonpartisan energy analysts are downplaying the chances of significant price easing in the weeks or months ahead. "In a typical year, the consumer would see a seasonal decline in gasoline prices as refiners switched from the more expensive summer grade gasoline to the less expensive winter grade formulation," Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, told Yahoo Finance. But "this has been anything but a typical year," he said, noting that substantial price increases in gasoline and diesel could be felt across a range of consumer goods and are "wiping out the season savings that the consumer has come to expect." GasBuddy's Patrick De Haan added in a recent blog post that the transition to cheaper winter-blend gasoline may help some, but "the scale of ongoing geopolitical escalations makes meaningful price relief unlikely in the near term." "Motorists should brace for continued volatility ahead." An acute problem for Trump Current gas prices are more than 35% higher than the $3.18 level where they sat at this stage of the 2024 election, when then-candidate Donald Trump regularly assailed Democrats over the issue. "We're going to bring your energy prices down," Trump promised at a campaign event almost exactly two years ago , one of countless times he slammed the Biden administration over the issue. In recent days, he has repeated his frequent promises of relief at the pump, saying oil prices will "drop like a rock" when the war in Iran ends and insisting that Ukraine needs to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries . President Donald Trump is seen at Shannon Airport after attending the final day of the Irish Open on September 13. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images The president briefly drove down diesel prices last Monday with a Truth Social post that claimed both Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop hitting energy targets. But the relief was short-lived when energy strikes from both countries continued . Last Tuesday saw another all-time record price for diesel, according to the American Automobile Association , at an average of nearly $6.27 per gallon. Trump is left with few options. Measures like restrictions on US oil exports energy experts have long suggested could backfire . Some Trump aides have downplayed the chances of an export ban, but the possibility is being closely watched. Charlie McElligott of Nomura Securities, in a note to clients, said an export ban could cut prices in the short term but lead to further price increases if refiners cut their capacity in response. Such a move, he said, would be akin to a "bomb being dropped on the global Economy." Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. item.title: U.S. floats AI warning system with China ahead of Trump-Xi summit
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met China's Vice Premier He Lifeng [Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent/X] Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday. Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York. The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week. AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach. "We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks. He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade. A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November. The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment. Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI. Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people." The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries. In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears abouts its potential negative impact on humanity. Trump has largely dismissed those concerns , arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China. He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins." In May, when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing, ways to collaborate on AI was one of the issues the two leaders discussed. Those talks ended with an agreement that China would buy Boeing jets and US agricultural goods in exchange for lower tariffs. item.title: Patrick Clancy opens up about forgiveness, grief and starting a new family
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Patrick Clancy spoke about coping with the deaths of his three children and how he has started rebuilding his life in his first televised interview since his ex-wife Lindsay Clancy's murder trial , The case has drawn widespread media attention, with the former labor and delivery nurse facing murder charges over the deaths of her three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — whom she admitted killing on Jan. 24, 2023. In an extensive interview with 60 Minutes aired on CBS News Sunday, Clancy said that at one point he "didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday," as he struggled with grief. He said that he still dreams about his children, telling interviewer Ross Douthat, "it's like I'm lucid in those dreams." Clancy also discussed how he met his now-wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, who also appeared in the show, and said false online conspiracy theories about his involvement in his children's deaths were "deeply harmful to the legacy of my children." Clancy and Dr. Danis confirmed they are starting a family together. Here are the key moments from the interview. 1. He and his new wife are having a baby Asked by correspondent Ross Douthat whether the couple was "starting a family" together, Dr. Danis replied, "Yeah," with Clancy adding that he "can't wait" to tell any future children about their brothers and sister. "I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids," he said. "And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister." On CBS Mornings on Monday, Douthat confirm that Dr. Danis was pregnant. "They are having a child," he said, acknowledging, "Maybe starting a family was too coy a way of asking it." 2. How Rachel Danis learned what had happened Dr. Danis, a fertility doctor, married Clancy in April this year. Joining her husband for the interview, she said that she first met him at a running club in New York in January 2024. She described finding out about his children while paying for coffee with Clancy during one of their meet-ups. "Pat pulled out his phone to pay, and I noticed this adorable photo of children as the wallpaper," she said. "And I just asked, 'Who are those cuties?' And Pat said, 'Those are my kids.' And then I think I asked if they live in Massachusetts, and Pat said, 'They died.' And this is just at the cashier." "I guess I had so many questions, and yet at the same time I didn't know exactly what to ask," she added. 3. He had a panic attack mid-testimony Clancy, who was the first witness to testify at his ex-wife's murder trial, told the court that when he returned from picking up food and prescriptions, he found his three children in the basement after calling 911 for Lindsay, who had jumped from a second-floor window. During the 60 Minutes special, he described having a panic attack mid-testimony and being put in an ambulance. "I went to a back room, and I started having this massive traumatic panic attack," he said. "My heart was pounding. And they put me in an ambulance. They offered me some medication, but I said, 'I — I don't want it, 'cause I want to go back and I want to finish this so I can be done with this.' And I went back and I finished the testimony." Recalling the 911 call being played in court, he said that "testifying is very difficult." "On the second day, a lot of that was focused on the night of January 24th. We did take a break right before they played the 911 call, which I knew was gonna be just horrific." The account rebuts what some online theorists interpreted as Clancy's stoicism on the stand, which in turn fueled conspiracy theories that he was somehow involved in the deaths of his children. These theories continued even after Clancy's lawyer warned he would take legal action against those responsible. Asked about the impact of the conspiracy theories circulating online , Clancy said, "It's painful to see. It makes it difficult to be in public, and it's possible that some of those people, after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it, and that's what we're left with." He said that the conspiracy theories are "deeply harmful to the legacy of my children." "It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health. And it's done real harm to real people, myself included but also others," he added. 4. He didn't expect to survive his own grief — and forgave his ex-wife While Patrick and Lindsay Clancy are no longer married, Patrick Clancy told CBS he had forgiven his ex-wife for what happened to their children. Asked if she had ever asked for his forgiveness, Clancy said, "No. But I gave it to her." "I saw headlines that said, you know, 'Killer Mom,' and 'Baby Murderer,' 'Monster.' And none of 'em were accurate. I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. Lindsay Clancy has been held at a state-run hospital since 2023. Greg Derr/via AP "And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside forever," he added. In the weeks following the tragedy, as Clancy tried to come to terms with life without his children, he discussed feeling so low that he had suicidal thoughts. "There was a time when I — I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday. And I was completely fine with it," he told the broadcaster. 5. Clancy's baby son died in his arms Two of the Clancys' children — Cora and Dawson — were declared dead on Jan. 24, but 8-month-old Callan remained alive for a few more days after being airlifted to Boston Children's Hospital. "I really thought there was a chance that Callan would live," he told 60 Minutes. "I remember just thinking, 'Just gimme one. Just gimme one kid,' and I would raise him as best I could, and I would give him the best life I possibly could. I'd tell him about his brother and sister. And I was holding out hope for that. "Then, when I got to the hospital, I saw the doctor. I saw the look on her face, and I knew that it wasn't going to be a good prognosis." During his final hours with Callan, Clancy said he sat and wrote tributes to each of his three children, typing with one hand while he held his baby's hand with the other. He told the program that he was afraid that if he didn't write about them, they would be forgotten. Callan's heart kept beating for four days before "he died in my arms," Clancy said. "I'm so grateful for those four days that I had with him. And I'm so grateful he hung on," he said. If you or someone you know is experiencing suicidal thoughts, call 911, or call the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-8255 or text HOME to the Crisis Text Line at 741741. item.title: Locals and lawmakers demand answers after ICE agent shoots DoorDash driver in Texas
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The victim, who was identified as a Venezuelan man, was transported to a local hospital and is in “in serious but stable condition." (Shahrzad Rasekh / Reuters) An ICE officer shot and seriously wounded a Venezuelan man Sunday afternoon as he was delivering food in Austin, Texas, his lawyer said. The man was taken to a local hospital and was “in serious but stable condition” after being shot in the torso, Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz said at a news conference earlier. The White House referred NBC News to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. A spokesperson for the DHS, the federal agency to which Immigration and Customs Enforcement belongs, said in a statement late Sunday that the man was stable and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S. Immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch identified him as Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, 28. He entered the country illegally under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal, the DHS spokesperson said, adding that Homeland Security Investigations, with help from the FBI, will lead an investigation into the shooting. The shooting occurred around 1 p.m. in North Austin. Texas Department of Public Safety spokesperson Sheridan Nolen said the agency received a request for assistance from ICE for a vehicle pursuit involving a blue Toyota Corolla. A social media video verified by NBC News captures the sound of tires screeching followed by a person exiting a dark-colored SUV as a blue sedan is stopped next to it, both vehicles facing one another. At least three gunshots are heard as the person approaches the sedan and runs up to it as it slowly lurches forward. The video shows the person standing next to the sedan’s driver’s side as it stops in front of an intersection. The sedan also appears to be damaged on the passenger side. A blue Toyota Corolla with visible bullet holes in a rear window, parked under an elevated stretch of Highway 183 in Austin, on Sunday. (Joel Angel Juarez / AP) The shooting occurred before DPS troopers arrived at the scene, Nolen said. “Once they arrived, DPS Troopers immediately began assisting partner law enforcement agencies in performing medical treatment on the driver of the Toyota Corolla,” she said in a statement. Lincoln-Goldfinch, who is representing the man, said lawyers for the hospital where he was treated indicated he had been released, though she wasn’t sure at the time to whom. Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez's wife said he was making a food delivery at the time of the incident Sunday. (via Refuerzo Collaborative) The hospital, Dell Seton Medical Center at The University of Texas, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Lincoln-Goldfinch said she was with his wife at the hospital earlier, hoping to get information on his condition, but they were escorted from the premises. “We are deeply concerned that his wife and family have not been permitted to see him and have not received a meaningful update regarding his current condition or whereabouts,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a statement. The man, who lives in Austin, is a DoorDash driver who was in the middle of a delivery when he was shot, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. In an email, a company spokesperson confirmed Garcés Perez was making a delivery at the time, adding that DoorDash is investigating and would not release more information “at this time.” Lincoln-Goldfinch told Telemundo Austin that her priority, and that of the man’s family, is to find him and verify his condition. “The main focus now is figuring out how and where he is, that he’s OK, and then we’ll be looking for justice,” she said. DHS has not provided any information about whether the ICE agent involved was wearing a body camera or if the man was the target of an operation or has any criminal background other than an immigration violation. Austin Mayor Kirk Watson said the Austin Police Department was not involved in the incident. Police Chief Lisa Davis said a “small foot pursuit” had occurred and that Austin police investigators were on the scene. Davis added that she was in contact with Homeland Security Investigations and other state law enforcement agencies. “A person being shot on the streets of Austin by someone purporting to be law enforcement, particularly when it’s ICE, is something that causes me to be unhappy and angry,” Watson said at the news conference. “While I’m unhappy and I’m angry about it, I’m not surprised at all.” Protesters who gathered at the site of the shooting on Sunday afternoon shouted anti-ICE slogans in English and Spanish. (Brandon Bell / Getty Images) Authorities deployed non-lethal weapons toward the crowd. (Joel Angel Juarez / AP) U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, demanded an independent investigation, the release of body camera footage and “accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law.” “Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened. We can see the lies with our own eyes. We will demand truth, transparency and accountability,” he said in a post on X . In a letter addressed to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting ICE Director David Venturella, Casar insisted on receiving a Congressional briefing by Sept. 28. James Talarico, who is running as the Democratic candidate for one of Texas’ U.S. Senate seats, said he is “closely following” reports of the shooting, and requested an investigation and all available footage. U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, demanded “full accountability.” “Trump has allowed ICE to flood our streets and put our communities in harms way again and again,” he said in a post on X . In reaction to the shooting, the League of United Latin American Citizens — the largest Latino civil rights organization in the U.S. — called on Congress to establish an independent oversight of immigration enforcement. The shooting comes two months after an ICE officer fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national, in Houston during an attempted traffic stop to conduct an immigration arrest. (Brandon Bell / Getty Images) Watson said he has asked for the city of Austin to be involved in any forthcoming investigations so that the police department can “be in a position to offer clear third-party eyes and expertise” In a statement, the Travis County District Attorney’s Office requested to be “co-equal partners in the investigation” and to receive cooperation from the federal government. Protesters who gathered at the site of the shooting on Sunday afternoon and evening, next to an elevated stretch of Highway 183, shouted anti-ICE slogans in English and Spanish. Some carried signs that said, “Stop ICE murder,” “Moms against ICE” and “Abolish ICE.” One woman, who said she has lived in Austin for 33 years, told NBC News earlier Sunday that she has never witnessed an incident like this and it “broke my heart.” The protest was punctuated with the sounds of drums, and someone could be heard saying, “They don’t want you to be here” via loudspeaker. Late Sunday night, the gathering roiled with tension, and Texas Department of Public Safety troopers responded by deploying tear gas and, in some instances, tackling protesters. Protesters had dispersed and troopers appeared to have exited the area by 11 p.m. local time. The shooting comes two months after an ICE officer fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national, in Houston during an attempted traffic stop to conduct an immigration arrest. DHS has said Salgado Araujo was in the country illegally and attempted to run over agents, but it has not provided evidence of its claims. This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/ice-shooting-austin-texas-rcna598870

item.title: Sen. Cassidy urges Trump to show 'radical honesty' about childhood vaccines
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen. Bill Cassidy (Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) Sen. Bill Cassidy on Sunday called on President Donald Trump to provide evidence for his claims about childhood vaccines, warning that discouraging immunization could result in more illnesses, hospitalizations, and deaths. The Louisiana Republican, a physician and chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, told CBS' "Face the Nation" that Trump should explain the basis for his proposal to split some childhood vaccines into multiple doses. "There needs to be, though, radical honesty," Cassidy said. "Have the president come forward. What is he basing this on? Who's giving him advice?" Trump said Friday that he would demand that drug companies split up children's vaccines into five doses, saying the change would lead to "a massive reduction in autism." Cassidy said he did not know which vaccines Trump was referring to or where the proposal originated. "If you want to be radically honest, the vaccines are safe," Cassidy said. "They've been proven to be safe." Cassidy warned that Trump's comments could have consequences because Americans listen to the president. "If he discourages immunization, there'll be fewer people immunized, and if we're speaking of measles, there'll be more people sick, in the hospital or even die," Cassidy said. Cassidy also said Heidi Overton, Trump's nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, would need to demonstrate at her confirmation hearing that she rejects Trump's characterization of the measles vaccine as lethal. "I need to hear that she understands that calling the measles vaccine lethal is absurd," Cassidy said. Cassidy pointed to recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania and a measles exposure at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia as evidence of the risks posed by the disease. "The president should be saying, 'Be vaccinated. It is safe and effective,'" Cassidy said. Asked whether the administration's vaccine messaging could hurt Republicans in the midterm elections, Cassidy cited polling showing strong support for childhood vaccination among women and said confusing public health messaging "probably does hurt." Cassidy also criticized Trump's proposal to provide $5,000 payments to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress in the midterm elections, calling the plan inflationary. "It's absolutely inflationary," Cassidy said. "If Joe Biden had proposed that, conservatives would have been all against it." Cassidy said borrowing money for the payments could put upward pressure on borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards. He instead called for action to reduce the national debt and address Social Security's finances. "We need to actually pay attention to our national debt," Cassidy said. Cassidy also weighed in on reports that Russian billionaire Umar Kremlev paid for portions of Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding celebrations in the Bahamas. The president said Friday that his son had repaid Kremlev. Cassidy, however, said repayment mattered but added that he would like to see it verified. "Anytime someone gives a $250,000 gift, and they have strong ties to the Kremlin, that's wrong," Cassidy said. "Even though in your mind it might be a gift, the appearance of it is really bad ... it shouldn't have been done in the first place." © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: The 'unprofessional' item Gen Z brings to interviews could be costing them jobs
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Proponents say a candidate's beverage of choice can help showcase their "personality." In today’s brutal job market, Gen Z is bringing their absolute A-game to interviews. But they’re also bringing their emotional support iced lattes. A generational debate has erupted online over a dead-simple question: Is waltzing into a job interview clutching an iced coffee completely unprofessional, or totally fine? The clash kicked off when TikTok corporate recruiter @caitlinrecruiter called out Gen Z candidates for arriving to interviews with iced lattes in hand. Drawing on her 16 years of experience placing candidates at Fortune 500 companies, she warned job seekers against the casual habit. “When you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte, it is perceived — from my opinion and a hiring standpoint—that this interview is just a stop on your list of errands for the day,” she alleged in the viral clip. “It looks like you went to Target, went to Starbucks, and now you’re stopping by your interview before moving on to the next thing.” She stood her ground, arguing that the beverage projects a casual and unserious attitude. Naturally, the internet picked sides and videos, posts, and comments flooded in as hiring managers and job seekers debated the iced coffee conundrum. Another creator chimed in, calling it “diabolical” to bring a “wet, plastic, condensation cup” into an interview room.” Putting it on a table leaves a messy water ring, they noted and called out the bad-look of taking loud slurps while trying to make a good first impression. Gen Z job seekers and their supporters are defending their right to stay caffeinated, and arguing they wouldn’t want to work anywhere where their choices are judged. “I don’t want to f–king work for you if you don’t want to hire me because I bring an iced coffee,” one Gen Z TikToker ranted, dismissing “traditional etiquette” as corporate brainwashing. Weighing in on the debate, LinkedIn News highlighted advice from professionals. Benjamin Chipman, a Gen Zer who works in marketing, advised interviewees who want to bring a drink to hold it in their left hand so their right hand remains dry for a handshake. He also said to avoid shaking the ice around and refrain from slurping the final drops. “Is this a generational thing?” asked communications manager Adam Raider. “I would NEVER bring an iced coffee… or a hot coffee… or tea, soda, juice, sangria… or any other beverage into a job interview. I WOULD accept water, if it was offered.” Only 43% of Gen Z prefer hot coffee, compared to 89% of adults over 60. matinee – stock.adobe.com One Gen Z TikToker explained the fight isn’t about the lattes, but about rejecting “arbitrary standards of professionalism” that have nothing to do with whether someone can actually do the job. Critics counter that clutching a fresh cold brew signals poor time management—proof you couldn’t even finish your morning coffee before rolling into the office. With US job postings for young adults aged 22 to 25 plunging 13% since 2022 across AI-exposed industries, Gen Z is already fighting an uphill battle. According to resumetemplates.com , about 4 in 10 hiring managers (41%) say Gen Z candidates show a general lack of professionalism, while 30% flag distraction. In an increasingly competitive market that isn’t doing favors for Gen Z work habits, that iced coffee might just cost them more than the five bucks it took to buy.
